“I was unable to do so, Bhante; I was negligent, Bhante.”
Question: But how, friends, was the experience of the suffering of hell by a being destined for hell explained there by the Blessed One?

Answer: Monks, when King Yama has questioned, interrogated, and exhorted him regarding the third divine messenger and remains silent, then, monks, the wardens of hell [subject him] to what is called the fivefold binding.

They inflict tortures upon him: they thrust a red-hot iron stake through one hand, they thrust a red-hot iron stake through the other hand, they thrust a red-hot iron stake through one foot, they thrust a red-hot iron stake through the other foot, and they thrust a red-hot iron stake through his midriff.
There, he experiences painful, intense, harsh, and bitter sensations.

“Venerable sir, by such statements as ‘He experiences [the result], yet he does not die until that evil kamma has been exhausted,’ the Blessed One there revealed the experience of the suffering of hell for one destined for hell.
This is a discourse intended to arouse spiritual urgency.
Question: But how, friend, was a discourse on the things that cause spiritual urgency delivered there by the Blessed One?
Answer: Once, monks, it occurred to King Yama: "It is said that those in the world who perform evil deeds undergo such various forms of torture. Oh, would that I might attain the human state!"
“May I obtain it, and may a Tathāgata, an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One, arise in the world”— in this way, venerable sir,
the Blessed One delivered a discourse intended to stir the heart there.
“Indeed, sir, those in the world who perform evil deeds...”
“Those young men who, being exhorted by the messengers of the gods, remain heedless, those men,
having entered a low state of existence, will grieve for a long time. But those virtuous, true persons here who [heed the messengers of the gods]...”
When urged, they never neglect the noble Dhamma.
Seeing danger in clinging, which gives rise to birth and death,
they are liberated through non-clinging in the destruction of birth and death.
“Those who are diligent and happy, having attained nibbāna in this very life,
have transcended all enmity and fear, and have gone beyond all suffering.
— *Catumahārājasutta*

Question: How was the eighth discourse, the *Catumahārājasutta*, spoken by the Blessed One—the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One—in the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*, in the third chapter (*Tikanipāta*), in the section on the messengers of the gods (*Devadūtavagga*)?

Answer: Regarding the eighth discourse, the *Catumahārājasutta*: "Bhikkhus, on the eighth day of the fortnight, the ministers and counselors of the Four Great Kings roam this world [to see] whether many people among humans..."
“‘They are devoted to their mothers, devoted to their fathers, devoted to recluses, devoted to brahmins, honoring those who are senior in their families;
they observe the Uposatha, they keep watch, and they perform meritorious deeds’—this is what was spoken by the Blessed One.

But few indeed, dear sir, among human beings are there those who are devoted to their mothers, devoted to their fathers, devoted to recluses, devoted to brahmins, honoring those who are senior in their families; who observe the Uposatha, keep watch, and perform meritorious deeds.”

“The divine hosts will surely diminish, and the asura hosts will surely increase!”—“Indeed, dear sir, among humans there are many who honor their mothers, honor their fathers, honor ascetics, honor brahmins, and respect the elders of the family; they observe the Uposatha, keep watch, and perform meritorious deeds.
“The divine hosts will surely increase, and the asura hosts will surely diminish!”
Ādhipateyya Sutta Question:
"In that same place, friend, how was the tenth discourse on dominance (ādhipateyya) spoken by the Blessed One?
Answer: "In that same place, Bhante, the tenth discourse on dominance was spoken thus: 'Monks, there are these three dominances.'"
"What are the three? Self-mastery, world-mastery, and Dhamma-mastery.

And what, monks, is self-mastery? Here, monks, a monk who has gone to the forest, or to the foot of a tree, or to an empty hut, reflects thus"—so it was said by the Blessed One, beginning with these words.

**Brāhmaṇavagga, Paribbājakasutta** **Question:** Venerable friend, concerning whom and on what occasion was the fourth discourse on wanderers (*paribbājakasutta*) in the *Brāhmaṇavagga* spoken by the Blessed One, and how was it delivered?
**Answer:** Venerable sir, the fourth discourse on wanderers in the *Brāhmaṇavagga* was spoken concerning a certain brahmin.
This was spoken concerning a wanderer. "Venerable sir, a certain brahmin wanderer said this to the Blessed One:
'Sir Gotama, it is said: "the Dhamma is definitive, the Dhamma is directly visible.
In what way, sir Gotama, is the Dhamma directly visible, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, and to be personally realized?'"

“...by the wise,” [it was said]. Regarding that matter, venerable sir, it has been said: “A person who is lustful, overcome by lust, with a mind obsessed by it, intends for his own affliction, intends for the affliction of others, and intends for the affliction of both;
he experiences mental pain and dejection. When lust is abandoned, he no longer intends for his own affliction, nor for the affliction of others...”
"He intends, he intends even for the affliction of both [self and others], yet he does not experience mental pain or dejection"—
this and more was spoken by the Blessed One in the *Vacchagottasutta*.
Question: Friend, concerning whom, on what occasion, and in what manner was the seventh discourse, the *Vacchagottasutta*, spoken by the Blessed One?
Answer: Venerable sir, the seventh discourse, the *Vacchagottasutta*, was spoken concerning the wanderer Vacchagotta.
Venerable sir, the wanderer Vacchagotta said this to the Blessed One: "I have heard this, Master Gotama..."
“The ascetic Gotama says thus: ‘Alms should be given only to me; alms should not be given to others.
(Repetition) We do not wish to misrepresent the venerable Gotama. Regarding that matter, Bhante, those who said, “Vaccha, the ascetic Gotama says thus:
‘Alms should be given only to me; alms should not be given to others’”—[they speak falsely].
Thus it was spoken by the Blessed One, beginning with these words.
**Question on the Saṅgāravasutta:** Venerable friend, concerning whom, on what occasion, and how was the tenth discourse, the *Saṅgāravasutta*, spoken by the Blessed One?
The Response: This tenth discourse, the *Saṅgāravasutta*, was spoken by the Blessed One concerning the brahmin Saṅgārava.
The brahmin Saṅgārava said this to the Blessed One: "Master Gotama, we who are called brahmins perform sacrifices and cause others to perform sacrifices.
In that regard, Master Gotama, both he who performs the sacrifice and he who causes it to be performed—"
They have practiced a manifold bodily course of merit, namely, by means of sacrifices. But as for this other person, Master Gotama,
from whatever family he has gone forth from the home life into homelessness, and who tames himself alone, composes himself alone,
and attains final Nibbāna alone— thus he has practiced a single bodily course of merit.

“...there is this, namely, the matter of going forth. Regarding that matter, venerable sir, the Blessed One spoke as follows: “In that case, brahmin, I shall question you about that very point; answer it as you see fit. [The brahmin replied:
“In this way too, Master Gotama, there is this practice of merit consisting in many bodily acts.”
Question: Friend, what kind of Dhamma teaching was given by the Blessed One at that very place during the second sequence?
Answer: Venerable sir, at that very place during the second sequence, the Blessed One gave a Dhamma teaching connected with the three kinds of wonders:
“Just as Master Gotama and Master Ānanda are, these are my objects of veneration; these are my objects of praise.”
“Just as Master Gotama and Master Ānanda are, so these are worthy of my honor and praise.
— *Mahāvagga*, *Venāgapura Sutta*.

Question: By that Blessed One... [as above] ...the Perfectly Enlightened One, in the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*, in the *Tikanipāta*, in the *Mahāvagga*, where, concerning whom, on what occasion, and how was the third *Venāgapura Sutta* spoken?
The Explanation: This was spoken, venerable sir, concerning the brahmin Vacchagotta of Venāgapura, in the brahmin village named Venāgapura among the Kosalans.
The brahmin Vacchagotta of Venāgapura said this to the Blessed One:
“It is wonderful, Master Gotama; it is marvelous, Master Gotama! To what extent, Master Gotama...”
“The faculties are serene, the complexion of the skin is pure and bright... (peyyāla)...
Surely, venerable Gotama, you must obtain high and luxurious beds and seats at will and without difficulty.
Regarding that matter, Bhante, [the Blessed One said]: “As for those high and luxurious beds and seats, Brahmin—namely, the *āsandi*...”
A couch, a woolen rug, a variegated coverlet, a cotton quilt, a feather mattress, a stuffed mattress, one with hair on both sides,
one with hair on one side only, a deer-skin rug, silk, embroidered cloth, an elephant-back rug, a horse-back rug, a chariot-seat rug, a spread made of antelope hide,
a choice spread made of kadali-deer skin, provided with a canopy and red cushions at both ends— these are difficult for those who have gone forth to obtain, and even if obtained...
“...are not permitted,” thus it was spoken by the Blessed One.
“It is wonderful, Master Gotama! It is marvelous, Master Gotama!
[The Blessed One spoke further: “Celestial high and luxurious beds.”
Question: And how, friend, was the divine high and luxurious bed and seat taught there by the Blessed One?
Answer: Here, brahmin, whatever village or town I am staying near, having dressed in the morning and taken my bowl and robe, I enter that very village or town for alms; and after the meal...
"Having returned from the alms-round, I shall enter the forest," and so forth— thus, venerable sir, did the Blessed One there teach the divine high and luxurious beds and seats.
This is the "Brahma High and Luxurious Beds and Seats."
Question: And how, friends, was the high and luxurious bed and seat taught there by the Blessed One?
Answer: Here, Brahmin, having dressed in the morning and taken bowl and robe, I enter that very village or town for alms, thinking: "I shall enter this village or town for alms"—and so forth.
"Venerable sir, the Exalted One has taught there the high and luxurious bed and seat.
But what, Master Gotama, is that high and luxurious bed and seat?
It is the noble high and luxurious bed and seat."
Question: And how, friend, was noble high and luxurious bedding taught there by the Blessed One?
Answer: Here, brahmin, whatever village or town I am staying near, having dressed in the morning and taken my bowl and robe, I enter that very village or town for alms. After the meal...
"Having returned from the alms round, I shall enter the forest itself"—it was in such words, venerable sir, that the Noble High and Grand Bed was taught there by the Blessed One.
Question: Friend, in that same Mahāvagga, where, concerning whom, on what occasion, and how was the fifth discourse, the Kesamutti Sutta, spoken by the Blessed One?
The Response: "Venerable sir, this was spoken concerning the Kālāmas of Kesamutta, a town of the Kālāmas in the Kosala country.
Venerable sir, the Kālāmas of Kesamutta said this to the Blessed One: 'Venerable sir, there are certain recluses and brahmins who come to Kesamutta;
they illuminate and exalt their own doctrine, while disparaging the doctrines of others...'"
"But they revile, deride, and despise us; they treat us with contempt. Furthermore, Bhante, other recluses and brahmins come to Kesamutta;
they too proclaim and illuminate their own doctrines, while they revile, deride, and despise the doctrines of others, treating them with contempt. Regarding this, Bhante, we have indeed a doubt."
“Doubt arises: ‘Who among these venerable recluses and brahmins has spoken the truth, and who has spoken falsehood?
In that matter, Bhante, the Blessed One spoke as follows: ‘It is fitting for you, Kālāmas, to doubt; it is fitting for you to be perplexed.
For it is at a point where one would doubt that doubt has arisen in you.’”
**Uposatha Sutta:

Questions** “Friend, where, concerning whom, and how was the tenth discourse on the Uposatha spoken by the Blessed One—the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One—in the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*, in the *Tika-nipāta*, in the *Mahāvagga*?
**Answer:** “At Sāvatthī, venerable sir, concerning Visākhā, Migāra’s mother, [the Blessed One spoke thus]: ‘There are three things, Visākhā...’”
“Uposatha. Which three? The cowherd’s uposatha, the Nigaṇṭha’s uposatha, and the noble one’s uposatha. Thus it was said by the Blessed One.
“Well then, Visākhā, from where have you come so early in the day?
“There are, Visākhā, three uposathas for me. Which three? The cowherd’s uposatha, the Nigaṇṭha’s uposatha, and the noble one’s uposatha.”
The Question on the Individual Gopālaka:
"And how, friends, was the Gopālaka Uposatha taught there by the Blessed One?
The Answer: "And how, Visākhā, is the Gopālaka Uposatha? Just as, Visākhā, at the time of evening, a cowherd..."
Having returned the cattle to their owners, he reflects:
"Today the cattle grazed in such-and-such places and drank water in such-and-such places;

tomorrow the cattle will graze in such-and-such places and drink water in such-and-such places. It was in this way, venerable sir, that the Blessed One explained the *gopālaka-uposatha* (the cattle-herder's observance).
Question on the Individual Nigaṇṭhas:
“And how, friends, was the Nigaṇṭha Uposatha explained there by the Blessed One?
Answer: “And how, Visākhā, is there the Nigaṇṭha Uposatha? There are, Visākhā, those of the ascetic class called Nigaṇṭhas.”
They thus exhort their disciple: "Come, good man! Lay down the rod against all living beings in the eastern direction up to a hundred leagues away;
lay down the rod against those in the western direction; those in the northern direction;
and those in the southern direction up to a hundred leagues away. Thus, venerable sir, they exhort him.
Therein, the Blessed One proclaimed the Nigaṇṭha Uposatha:
"Come, good man;
come, good man, having cast off all your clothes, speak thus."
I am not the owner of anything anywhere, nor does anything anywhere belong to me.
This is the Noble Uposatha.
Question: Friend, how was the Noble Uposatha explained by the Blessed One there in detail?
The Response: And how, Visākhā, is there the noble Uposatha? It is the cleansing by effort of a defiled mind.
And how, Visākhā, is there the cleansing by effort of a defiled mind?
Here, Visākhā, a noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata thus: "Indeed, that Blessed One..."
“He is the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One, endowed with knowledge and conduct, the Well-Gone, the Knower of the World, the Unsurpassed Leader of persons to be tamed,
the Teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. As he recollects the Tathāgata in this way, his mind becomes serene, joy arises,
and those defilements of the mind are abandoned— thus it is said there, venerable sir.
The Blessed One has explained the noble Uposatha in detail.
Question: But how, friend, has the Blessed One described the great fruitfulness, the great benefit of the noble Uposatha when it is observed in this way?
Answer: To what extent is it of great fruit, to what extent is it of great benefit, to what extent is it of great radiance, and to what extent is it of great pervasiveness?
Just as if, Visākhā, one were to exercise sovereignty, lordship, and kingship over these sixteen great populous realms,
namely: Aṅga, Magadha, Kāsi, Kosala, Vajjī, Malla, Cetī,
Vaṅga, Kuru, Pañcāla, Maccha, Sūrasena, Assaka, Avantī, and Gandhāra.

“Venerable sir, by such statements as ‘It does not amount to even a sixteenth part of the eightfold uposatha of the Kambhojas,’ the Blessed One has there described the great fruitfulness and great benefit of the noble uposatha observed in that manner.”—
Ānandavagga.

**Ājīvakasutta** **Question:** In the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*, in the third collection (*Tikanipāta*), in the section on Ānanda (*Ānandavagga*), where was the second *Ājīvakasutta* spoken, concerning whom, on what subject,
by whom, and how? **Answer:** It was spoken, venerable sir, at Kosambī, concerning a certain householder who was a follower of the Ājīvakas, by the Venerable Ānanda.
This was spoken by the Elder Ānanda, the keeper of the Dharma-treasury. "Venerable sir, a certain householder who was a lay follower of the Ājīvakas said this to the Venerable Ānanda:
'Venerable Ānanda, whose Dhamma is well-expounded? Who in the world are practicing rightly? Who in the world have performed their task well?
Regarding that matter, venerable sir, [Ānanda said]: 'In that case, householder, I shall question you about this very point.'"
“Please explain it in such a way that it may be acceptable to you,” said the Venerable Ānanda Thera, the Dhamma-treasurer, and so forth.
“Venerable Ānanda, whose Dhamma is well-expounded? Who in the world are practicing rightly? Who in the world have performed their duty well?
“What do you think, householder? [the Blessed One asked].
“In this way, householder, you have explained this.
“Magnificent, Bhante! Magnificent, Bhante! Just as, Bhante, one might set upright what had been overturned...
— *Gandhajātasutta*
Question: Regarding that very ninth discourse on types of fragrance, venerable friend, with reference to whom, on what occasion, and how was it spoken by the Blessed One?
Answer: It was spoken, venerable sir, with reference to the Venerable Ānanda. The Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
"There are these three kinds of fragrances, venerable sir, whose scent travels only with the wind and not against the wind... [as above]... "
“Is there, venerable sir, any kind of fragrance whose scent travels with the wind,
whose scent travels against the wind, and whose scent travels both with and against the wind? “In this regard, Ānanda,
there is indeed such a fragrance whose scent travels with the wind, whose scent travels against the wind...”
"The fragrance travels with the wind, against the wind, and even crosswise," so it was said by the Blessed One.
"The fragrance of flowers does not travel against the wind,
nor does that of sandalwood, tagara, or jasmine."
The fragrance of the virtuous wafts even against the wind;
the person of integrity pervades all directions.
(The Donkey Sutta)
Question: Friend, how was the second *Gadrabha Sutta* (Ass Sutta) spoken by the Blessed One in the *Samaṇa-vagga*?
Answer: Bhante, in the *Samaṇa-vagga*, the second *Gadrabha Sutta* is as follows:
“Bhikkhus, just as a donkey follows closely behind a herd of cattle, thinking, ‘I too am being tamed; I too am being tamed,’ yet it is not [tamed].”
“His color was just like that of oxen, his voice was not like that of oxen, and his gait was not like that of oxen;
he followed right behind the herd of oxen, saying, ‘I too am to be tamed!
I too am to be tamed! Thus it was spoken by the Blessed One, and so forth.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
"We will have intense desire for undertaking the training in higher virtue... [and so on] ...for undertaking the training in higher wisdom"—thus, from the Saṅkavāsutta.
Question: Friend, where, concerning whom, on what occasion, and how was the eleventh sutta, the Saṅkavāsutta, spoken by the Blessed One?
Answer: Lord, it was spoken among the Kosalans at a Kosalan town named Saṅkavā, concerning a monk of the Kassapa clan.
Lord, that monk of the Kassapa clan, having offended the Blessed One in mind, [addressed] the Blessed One...
In his presence, he confessed his transgression as a transgression. Regarding that matter, O Bhante, [the Blessed One said]:
"Kassapa, even if a monk who is an elder is not desirous of training and does not speak in praise of undertaking the training;
and if he does not encourage other monks who are not desirous of training to undertake the training; and if he does not speak in praise of those other monks who are desirous of training..."
"That which has come to be is pleasant in its time"— thus was it spoken by the Blessed One, and so forth.
From the *Loṇakapallavagga*,
the *Accāyikasutta*.

Question: Friend... [as above] ...how was the first *Accāyika-sutta* spoken by the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, in the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*, in the *Tika-nipāta*, in the *Loṇakapalla-vagga*?
Answer: Venerable sir, in the *Loṇakapalla-vagga*, the first *Accāyika-sutta* is as follows:
"Monks, there are these three urgent duties for a householder who is a farmer. Which three? Here, monks, a farmer..."
Householder, he very quickly prepares the field well-plowed and well-tilled.
Having very quickly prepared the field well-plowed and well-tilled, he very quickly sows the seeds.
Having very quickly sown the seeds, he very quickly brings water to it and also carries it away. These, monks, are the three...
“...there are urgent duties for a householder who is a farmer,” thus it was said by the Blessed One, venerable sir,
in the *Ruṇṇasutta* of the *Sambodhavagga*.
Question: But, friend, how was the fifth sutta on weeping in the Sambodha-vagga spoken by the Blessed One?
Answer: Bhante, the fifth sutta on weeping in the Sambodha-vagga was spoken thus:
"Monks, this is weeping in the discipline of the Noble One, namely, singing; monks, this is madness in the discipline of the Noble One, namely, dancing; monks, this is childishness..."
“Monks, in the discipline of the Noble One, this is what is meant by excessive laughing with bared teeth:
therefore, monks, there is the destruction of the bridge for song, the destruction of the bridge for dance; enough for you who are delighted by the Dhamma to smile merely as a smile.
Thus, venerable sir, was it spoken by the Blessed One.
**Arakkhīkasutta** **Question:** Venerable sir, where, concerning whom, and how was the seventh sutta, the *Arakkhitasutta*, spoken by the Blessed One?
**Answer:** At Sāvatthī, venerable sir, concerning the householder Anāthapiṇḍika, [it was spoken thus]: "Householder, when the mind is unprotected..."
“Bodily action is unprotected, verbal action is unprotected, and mental action is unprotected. For one whose bodily action is unprotected,
whose verbal action is unprotected, and whose mental action is unprotected, the bodily action becomes defiled, the verbal action becomes defiled,
and the mental action becomes defiled”— thus it was spoken by the Blessed One, and so forth.
Question: Venerable friend, how was the sixth sutta in the Āpāyikavagga, the *Apaṇṇakasutta*, spoken by the Blessed One?
The Answer—In the *Āpāyika-vagga*, venerable sir, is the sixth discourse, the *Apaṇṇaka-sutta*:
“Monks, there are these three failures. Which three? Failure in virtue, failure in mind, and failure in view. And what, monks, is failure in virtue?
Here, monks, a certain person destroys life... [and so on] ...he is a speaker of idle chatter. This, monks, is called...”
“Failure in virtue,” and so forth, was spoken by the Blessed One.
(From the *Kusināra Sutta* in the *Kusināravagga*).
Question: But, friend, in the Kusināra Chapter, where, concerning whom, and how was the first Kusināra Sutta spoken by the Blessed One?
Answer: At Kusinārā, venerable sir, in the Baliharaṇa Grove, concerning a number of bhikkhus, [it was spoken] thus:
"Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu dwells dependent upon a certain village or town. Then a householder..."
“Or a householder’s son, having approached, invites [him] for a meal on the following day”—thus was it spoken by the Blessed One, beginning with these words.
Question: Friend, in that very same place, where, with whom, and how was the fifth discourse, the *Hatthaka-sutta*, spoken by the Blessed One?
The Response: In Sāvatthī, venerable sir, the Blessed One spoke thus to the young deva Hatthaka:
"Hatthaka, those qualities that were active when you were formerly a human being—do they still function for you now? and so forth.
This is the Anuruddha Sutta.
Question: Regarding that very same [discourse], friend, with whom was the eighth discourse, the Anuruddha Sutta, spoken, and by whom?

Answer: Venerable sir, the eighth discourse, the Anuruddha Sutta, was spoken concerning the Venerable Elder Anuruddha by the Venerable Elder Sāriputta, the General of the Dhamma: "Friend Anuruddha, when it occurs to you thus..."
‘With the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, I survey a thousand worlds’—
this is what you have in mind,” he said.
“It would be well indeed if the Venerable Anuruddha, having abandoned these three things and not attending to these three things, were to direct his mind toward the deathless element.”
Kusīnārā Chapter:
Paṭicchanna Sutta.

Question: Venerable friend, how was the ninth discourse, the *Paṭicchanna Sutta*, spoken by the Blessed One—the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One—in the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*, in the Section of Threes, in the Kusīnārā Chapter?
The Response—The Ninth Discourse on Concealment: “Monks, these three things bring results when they are concealed, not when they are revealed.
Which three? Monks, women bring results when they are concealed, not when they are revealed;
monks, the mantras of the brahmins bring results when they are concealed, not when they are revealed; monks, wrong view brings results when it is concealed...”
“They bring concealment, not disclosure. “Monks, these three things, monks, bring concealment, not disclosure.
Thus it was spoken by the Blessed One, beginning with this, in the *Lekhasutta*.
Question: In that very context, friend, how was the tenth Discourse on Scratches (Lekhasutta) spoken by the Blessed One?
Answer: Regarding the tenth Discourse on Scratches, venerable sir: “Bhikkhus, these three persons are found existing in the world.
Which three? A person like a scratch on stone, a person like a scratch on earth, and a person like a scratch on water.”
The person. And what, monks, is the person who is like a mark on stone?
Here, monks, a certain person is prone to anger frequently, and that anger of his persists for a long time.
Just as, monks, a mark on stone is not quickly worn away by wind or water, but remains for a long time, even so...
"Monks, here a certain person is frequently angry, and that anger of his persists for a long time. This, monks,
is called a person comparable to a scratch on a stone," thus it was spoken by the Blessed One, beginning with these words,
in the *Yodhājīvavagga*.
**Question:** But, friend, how was the fifth sutta in the *Yodhājīva-vagga*, the *Kesakambala-sutta*, spoken by the Blessed One?
**Answer:** In the *Yodhājīva-vagga*, venerable sir, the fifth *Kesakambala-sutta* begins: “Bhikkhus, just as if... [the Blessed One spoke thus].”
"Of all garments woven on a loom, a blanket of human hair is declared to be the most wretched.
A blanket of human hair, monks, is cold in the cold, hot in the heat, ugly, foul-smelling, and unpleasant to the touch.
In the same way, monks, of all the doctrines of various recluses and brahmins, the doctrine of Makkhali is declared to be the most wretched."
Thus was it spoken by the Blessed One.
From the Maṅgala-vagga,
the Vandanā-sutta.
Question: But, friend, how was the ninth discourse on veneration in the Chapter on Blessings spoken by the Blessed One?
Answer: In the Chapter on Blessings, venerable sir, the ninth discourse on veneration was spoken thus:
“Bhikkhus, there are these three kinds of veneration. Which three? By body, by speech, and by mind. These, bhikkhus, are the three kinds of veneration. Thus it was.
"Venerable sir, this was said by the Blessed One:
‘Monks, there are these three kinds of homage. Which three? By body, by speech, and by mind. These, monks, are the three kinds of homage.
(The Pubbaṇha Sutta)
Question: In that regard, friend, how was the tenth *Pubbaṇhasutta* spoken by the Blessed One?
Answer: Regarding the tenth *Pubbaṇhasutta*, venerable sir:
"Bhikkhus, those beings who, in the morning time, practice good conduct of body, practice good conduct of speech, and practice good conduct of mind—for them, the morning is well-spent."

"Monks, it is so for those beings... Monks, those beings who at the time of midday—and so on—up to—at the time of evening, practice good conduct with the body, practice good conduct with speech, and practice good conduct with the mind—for those beings, monks, the evening is auspicious.
Thus, venerable sir, was it spoken by the Blessed One.
A good star, a good auspicious sign, a good dawn, a good rising;
a good moment, a good hour, and what is well-offered to those who lead the holy life.
(Bhaṇḍagāmavagga)
**Anubuddhasutta** **Question:** But, friend, in the Catukkanipāta, within the Bhaṇḍagāmavagga, how was the first *Anubuddhasutta* spoken by the Blessed One concerning the Teacher?
**Answer:** Regarding many bhikkhus at Bhaṇḍagāma among the Vajjīs, O Bhante, [the Blessed One spoke] concerning the four [qualities]: "Bhikkhus, there are these four... [and so forth].
“Through non-comprehension and non-penetration of phenomena, monks, this long course has been run and this long cycle undergone by both you and me.

Of which four phenomena? Through non-comprehension and non-penetration of noble virtue, monks, this long course has been run and this long cycle undergone by both you and me. Monks, [of noble virtue...]
"Because of the non-awakening and non-penetration of concentration... of noble wisdom, monks...
and of noble liberation, monks, this long journey has been traversed and wandered through by both me and you," thus it was spoken by the Blessed One, venerable sir, and so forth.
Pu: Friend, how was the sixth Discourse on the One of Little Learning spoken by the Blessed One right there? Vi:
In that regard, Bhante, the sixth Discourse on the One of Little Learning [begins]: "Bhikkhus, these four types of persons are found existing in the world..."
"In the world. Which four? One who has heard little and is not proficient in what he has heard; one who has heard little and is proficient in what he has heard;

one who has heard much and is not proficient in what he has heard; and one who has heard much and is proficient in what he has heard. Thus it was spoken by the Blessed One, beginning with these words, in the Caravagga.
Pu: But, friend, how was the first discourse in the Chapter on Wandering (*Caravagga*), the *Carasutta*, spoken by the Blessed One? Vi:
Venerable sir, in the Chapter on Wandering, the first discourse, the *Carasutta*, [begins]: “Monks, if even while a monk is walking, there arises in him...”
"Whether it be a thought of sensual desire, a thought of ill will, or a thought of cruelty— if a bhikkhu tolerates such a thought,
does not abandon it, does not dispel it, does not bring it to an end, and does not cause it to cease," so it was said by the Blessed One in the Uruvelavagga.

Lokasutta (First) – “In this regard, friends... [as before] ...how was the third discourse on the world spoken by the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, in the Aṅguttara Nikāya, in the Catukka Nipāta, in the Uruvela Vagga?
[The Venerable Mahākaccāna replied: “In the Uruvela Vagga, Bhante, the third discourse on the world, ‘The world, bhikkhus, has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata,’ was spoken.”
The Tathāgata is detached from the world, monks; the origin of the world has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata, and the origin of the world has been abandoned by the Tathāgata;
the cessation of the world, monks, has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata, and the cessation of the world has been realized by the Tathāgata;
the path leading to the cessation of the world, monks, has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata.
"The path leading to the cessation of the world has been developed by the Tathāgata"—thus, venerable sir, it was spoken by the Blessed One, beginning with these words.
"The Tamed is the best among those who tame;
the Peaceful is the sage among those who have attained peace."
The foremost among those who have been liberated,
the best among those who have crossed over—
having directly known the entire world.
All in the world as it truly is;
detached from the whole world,
unattached to the entire world.
He is indeed the hero who has overcome all,
the liberator from all fetters;
when questioned, he [attains] supreme peace.
Nibbāna is free from fear from any quarter.
This one is the Buddha whose taints are exhausted,
free from affliction, and with doubts severed.
Having reached the destruction of all karma,
liberated through the exhaustion of the substrata—
this is that Blessed One, the Buddha.
This lion, the unsurpassed one,
has set in motion the Wheel of Brahma in the world together with its devas.
Thus gods and humans alike,
who have gone for refuge to the Buddha,
come together and pay homage to him.
Great, free from timidity.
Tamed, he is the best among those who tame;
peaceful, the sage is the best among those who seek peace.
The foremost among those who have been liberated,
the best among those who have crossed over—
thus indeed do they pay homage to him.
Great and free from timidity;
in this world with its devas,
there is no one who is my equal.
Brahmacariyasutta Pu—In that very place, friend, how was the fifth Discourse on the Holy Life spoken by the Blessed One?
Vi—The fifth Discourse on the Holy Life, venerable sir, begins: "Monks, this holy life is not lived..."

"It is not for the sake of deceiving people, nor for the sake of flattering people, nor for the sake of the benefits of gain, honor, and fame, nor for the sake of the benefit of escaping through mere talk,
nor with the thought, 'Let people know me thus. Rather, monks, this holy life is lived for the sake of restraint, for the sake of abandoning, for the sake of dispassion,
and for the sake of cessation"— thus was it spoken by the Blessed One, and so forth.
Pu: Friend, how was the eighth discourse on the Noble Lineages (Ariyavaṃsasutta) spoken by the Blessed One? Vi:
Venerable sir, in that very place the eighth discourse on the Noble Lineages was spoken thus: "Bhikkhus, there are these four noble lineages, the foremost..."

These four, monks, are ancient, traditional, and long-standing; they are unmixed, have not been mixed in the past, will not be mixed, and are not censured by wise recluses and brahmins. What are the four?
Here, monks, a monk is content with any kind of robe, he speaks in praise of being content with any kind of robe, and he does not, for the sake of a robe, engage in improper search.

He does not engage in what is unbecoming; he does not become anxious when he has not obtained a robe, and when he has obtained a robe, he uses it without attachment, without infatuation, without craving, seeing the danger and discerning the escape.
Furthermore, through that contentment with whatever robe he may have, he neither exalts himself nor disparages others. For whoever therein is skillful, diligent, clearly comprehending, and mindful—
“This, monks, is called a monk who stands firm in the ancient, primordial noble lineage,” thus it was spoken by the Blessed One, beginning with these words.
(Cakkavagga,
Cakkasutta)
Pu: But, friend, how was the first *Cakkasutta* in the *Cakkavagga* spoken by the Blessed One?
Vi: Venerable sir, in the *Cakkavagga*, the first *Cakkasutta* states: "Bhikkhus, there are these four wheels;
for gods and humans who possess them, the fourfold wheel turns, and for gods and humans who possess them, before long..."
“They attain greatness and abundance in wealth. What are the four?
Dwelling in a suitable locality, association with superior persons, right self-application, and merit performed in the past. Thus it was spoken by the Blessed One in the *Saṅgaha Sutta*.
Pu: "Friend, how was the second Discourse on the Bases of Conciliation spoken by the Blessed One?

Vi: "Venerable sir, the second Discourse on the Bases of Conciliation was spoken by the Blessed One as follows: 'Bhikkhus, there are these four bases of conciliation. What are the four? Generosity, kindly speech, beneficial conduct, and impartiality. Thus it was spoken by the Blessed One. This is the Sīha-sutta.
Pu: "Friend, how was the third *Sīha-sutta* spoken by the Blessed One?
Vi: "In that very place, Bhante, the third *Sīha-sutta* [states]: 'Bhikkhus, the lion, the king of beasts, comes out from his lair in the evening;
having come out from his lair, he stretches himself; having stretched himself, he surveys the four quarters.'"
"Having surveyed the four directions all around, he roars his lion’s roar three times; having roared his lion’s roar three times, he sets out for his almsround.
Thus it was spoken by the Blessed One in the *Doṇasutta*.

Pu—Venerable friend, where, concerning whom, on what basis, and how was the sixth discourse, the *Doṇasutta*, spoken by the Blessed One... pe ...the Fully Enlightened One in the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*, in the Fourth Book (*Catukkanipāta*), in the Chapter on the Wheel (*Cakkavagga*)?
Vi—It was spoken, venerable sir, between Ukkaṭṭha and Setavyā, concerning the brahmin Doṇa.
Venerable sir, the brahmin Doṇa said this to the Blessed One: "May you, sir, become our king. It was concerning him [that it was spoken].
Venerable sir, regarding this matter, the Blessed One spoke thus: "Indeed, brahmin, I shall not become a deva," and so forth.
[The brahmin said: "It is wonderful indeed, sir! It is marvelous indeed, sir! These are surely not the footprints of one who has been a human being.
You, sir, will become a deva."
“I shall not become a deva, brahmin.
“Then will you become a gandhabba?
“I shall not become a gandhabba, brahmin.”
Ujjayasutta (Pu) – Regarding this, friend, how was the ninth Ujjayasutta spoken by the Blessed One?
Vi – The ninth, Bhante, the Ujjayasutta: “Indeed, Brahmin, I do not praise every sacrifice; nor... [does he praise] all asceticism.”
"But, brahmin, I do not praise every kind of sacrifice.

For instance, brahmin, in a sacrifice where cattle are slaughtered, goats and sheep are slaughtered, chickens and pigs are slaughtered, and various living beings meet their destruction"—this is what was spoken by the Blessed One.
"Does Master Gotama also praise such a sacrifice?"
Friend, how was the first Discourse on the Development of Concentration in the Rohitassa Chapter spoken by the Blessed One?
Venerable sir, in the Rohitassa Chapter, the first Discourse on the Development of Concentration states: "Monks, there are these four developments of concentration.
What are the four? There is, monks, a development of concentration that, when developed and cultivated, leads to a pleasant dwelling in this very life;
there is, monks, a development of concentration that, when developed and cultivated, leads to the attainment of knowledge and vision."
"It conduces [to this], monks; there is, monks, a development of concentration which, when developed and cultivated, conduces to mindfulness and clear comprehension;
there is, monks, a development of concentration which, when developed and cultivated, conduces to the destruction of the taints"—thus it was spoken by the Blessed One, and so forth.
Pu: Friend, how was the second Discourse on the Exposition of Questions spoken by the Blessed One in that very place? Vi:
Venerable sir, in that very place the second Discourse on the Exposition of Questions was spoken thus: "Bhikkhus, there are these four ways of answering questions."
"What are the four? There is, monks, a question to be answered categorically;
there is, monks, a question to be answered analytically; there is, monks, a question to be answered with a counter-question;
there is, monks, a question to be set aside"—thus it was spoken by the Blessed One, beginning with these words.
Puññābhisandavagga,
First Saṃvāsasutta:
Friend, where, concerning whom, and how was the third Saṃvāsasutta spoken by the Blessed One in the Puññābhisandavagga?

“Venerable sir, in the *Puññābhisanda-vagga*, the third discourse on cohabitation (*Saṃvāsa-sutta*), delivered between Madhurā and Verañjā concerning many householders and householder women, [the Blessed One said]: ‘Householders, there are these four types of cohabitation.
What are the four? A wretch cohabits with a wretch; a wretch cohabits with a goddess;’”
“The god dwells together with the female spirit; the god dwells together with the goddess”—thus was it spoken by the Blessed One, and so forth.

Pu: Venerable friend, how was the fifth discourse, the *Samajīvisutta*, spoken by the Blessed One—the Arahant, the Fully Enlightened One—in the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*, in the fourth chapter (*Catukkanipāta*), in the section on the flow of merit (*Puññābhisanda-vagga*)?

“Vi—The fifth, Bhante, is the Samajīvisutta: ‘Householders, if both husband and wife should desire to see one another both in this present life and in the future life, they should both have equal faith, equal virtue, equal generosity, and equal wisdom;
then they will see one another both in this present life and in the future life.’”
"And they see one another in the future life," thus it was spoken by the Blessed One in the *Pattakammavagga*,
in the *Ānaṇyasukhasutta*.
Pu: But, friend, in the *Pattakamma-vagga*, where, concerning whom, and how was the second *Ānañjasukha-sutta* spoken by the Blessed One?
Vi: Venerable sir, in the *Pattakamma-vagga*, the second *Ānañjasukha-sutta* was spoken at Sāvatthī concerning the householder Anāthapiṇḍika:
"Householder, there are these four kinds of happiness to be attained by a layperson who enjoys sensual pleasures..."
"From time to time, depending on the occasion, there are four [kinds of happiness]. Which four?
The happiness of possession, the happiness of enjoyment, the happiness of debtlessness, and the happiness of blamelessness"—thus it was spoken by the Blessed One.
Having understood the happiness of debtlessness, and then the supreme happiness of possession...
A mortal enjoying the pleasure of wealth, through that [experience] wisdom perceives clearly;
perceiving clearly, the wise one understands both sides:
this [pleasure of wealth] is not worth even a sixteenth part of the happiness that is blameless.
Appaṇṇakavagga,
Sappurisasutta: "But,
friend, how was the third discourse on the true person (Sappurisasutta) spoken by the Blessed One in the Appaṇṇakavagga?"
Vi—In the *Apaṇṇakavagga*, venerable sir, the third discourse on the true person (*sappurisasutta*) was spoken by the Blessed One as follows:
“Bhikkhus, one who possesses four qualities is to be known as a person of no integrity (*asappurisa*). Which four?
Here, bhikkhus, a person of no integrity reveals the dispraise of another even when unasked, let alone when asked,” and so forth.

“We shall dwell with a mind like that of a newly arrived bride”—thus was the seventh Discourse on the Inconceivable spoken by the Blessed One right there, friends. This is the *Acinteyyasutta* (Pu). Thus was it spoken by the Blessed One.

“Vi—The seventh, O Bhante, is the Acinteyya Sutta: ‘Monks, there are these four inconceivable things that should not be pondered, for one who ponders them would partake of madness and vexation. What are the four?
Monks, the Buddha-range of the Buddhas is inconceivable and should not be pondered; one who ponders it would partake of madness and vexation.’”
Thus was it spoken by the Blessed One.
From the *Macalavagga*,
the *Tamotamasutta*.
Pu: But, friend, how was the fifth sutta, the *Tamotamasasutta*, spoken by the Blessed One in the Macala Chapter?

Vi: Venerable sir, in the Macala Chapter, the fifth sutta, the *Tamotamasasutta*, [states]: "Bhikkhus, there are these four types of persons found existing in the world. Which four? One who goes from darkness to darkness; one who goes from darkness to light; one who goes from light to darkness; and one who goes from light to light."
“Light unto light, the ultimate goal of light”— thus it was spoken by the Blessed One.
From the *Asura-vagga*,
the *Asura-sutta*.

Pu: "Friend, how was the first Discourse on Asuras spoken by the Blessed One... the Perfectly Enlightened One, in the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*, in the Section of Fours (*Catukkanipāta*), in the Chapter on Asuras (*Asuravagga*)?
Vi: "Venerable sir, in the Chapter on Asuras, the first Discourse on Asuras states: 'Bhikkhus, there are these four types of persons found existing in the world.
Which four? The asura with an asura retinue; the asura with a deva retinue; the deva with an asura retinue; [and the deva with a deva retinue].'"
“A god surrounded by a retinue of gods”—thus it was spoken by the Blessed One, and so forth.
Regarding the *Samādhisutta*:
Friend, how was the fourth discourse on concentration (*samādhisutta*) spoken by the Blessed One right there?
VI—The fourth Discourse on Concentration: "Bhante, there are these four persons found existing in the world.
Which four? Here, bhikkhus, a certain person gains internal serenity of mind but does not gain the higher wisdom of insight into phenomena.
But here, bhikkhus, another person gains the higher wisdom of insight into phenomena..."
"One does not obtain internal tranquility of mind. But here, monks, a certain person neither obtains internal tranquility of mind nor obtains higher wisdom and insight into phenomena.
And here, monks, a certain person both obtains internal tranquility of mind and obtains higher wisdom and insight into phenomena."
Thus was it spoken by the Blessed One and so forth.
Regarding the *Rāgavinaya-sutta*:
Friend, how was the sixth discourse on the subduing of lust spoken by the Blessed One in that very place?
VI – The sixth discourse on the removal of lust, Bhante: “Bhikkhus, there are these four persons found existing in the world. Which four?
One who practices for his own benefit but not for the benefit of others; one who practices for the benefit of others but not for his own benefit;
one who practices neither for his own benefit nor for the benefit of others; and one who practices both for his own benefit and for the benefit of others.”
Thus it was spoken by the Blessed One, beginning with these words.
*Valāhakavagga*,
First *Valāhakasutta*.
Pu: Friend, in the Valāhaka Vagga, where, concerning whom, and how was the first discourse on clouds spoken by the Blessed One?
Vi: At Sāvatthī, venerable sir, concerning a number of bhikkhus, [it was spoken thus]: "Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of clouds. Which four? Those that thunder but do not rain;
those that rain but do not thunder; those that neither thunder nor rain; [and those that both thunder and rain]."
“Those that thunder but do not rain; those that rain but do not thunder; those that neither thunder nor rain; and those that both thunder and rain. These, monks, are the four clouds.
In the same way, monks, there are four types of persons resembling clouds existing in the world. Which four? One who thunders but does not rain;
one who rains but does not thunder; one who neither thunders nor rains; and one who both thunders and rains.”
Thus was it spoken by the Blessed One.
Regarding the *Udakarahada Sutta*:
"In that very place, friend, how was the fourth *Udakarahada Sutta* spoken by the Blessed One?"
“Venerable sir, this is the fourth Discourse on the Ponds. ‘Monks, there are these four ponds. Which four?
One that is shallow but appears deep; one that is deep but appears shallow; one that is shallow and appears shallow;
and one that is deep and appears deep. These, monks, are the four ponds. In the same way, monks, there are four [persons] comparable to ponds.’”
“There are four types of persons found existing in the world. Which four? One who is shallow but appears deep;

one who is deep but appears shallow; one who is shallow and appears shallow; and one who is deep and appears deep. Thus it was spoken by the Blessed One, beginning with these words, in the *Mūsikasutta*.
Pu: "Friend, how was the seventh Discourse on the Mouse spoken by the Blessed One in that very place?
Vi: "The seventh Discourse on the Mouse, Bhante, is as follows: 'Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of mice. Which four?

The one that digs a burrow but does not dwell in it; the one that dwells in a burrow but does not dig it; the one that neither digs a burrow nor dwells in one; and the one that both digs a burrow and dwells in it.'"

"The maker and the dweller. These, monks, are the four kinds of mice. In the same way, monks, there are four types of persons resembling mice found existing in the world. Which four? One who makes a footing but does not dwell [therein];
one who dwells [therein] but does not make a footing; one who neither makes a footing nor dwells [therein]; and one who both makes a footing and dwells [therein]."
Thus was it spoken by the Blessed One.
Friend, having extracted certain discourses from the *Aṅguttara Nikāya* and the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*, I shall question you regarding them.

For the increase of the learning of the many people. Friend, how was the eighth discourse, the *Balībaddha-sutta*, spoken by the Blessed One in the *Valāhaka-vagga* of the Fourth Chapter (*Catukkanipāta*) of the *Saṃgīta-aṅguttaranikāya*?
Venerable sir, in the *Valāhaka-vagga*, the eighth discourse, the *Balībaddha-sutta*, states: “Monks, there are these four oxen.”
Which four? One who is fierce toward his own cattle but not toward the cattle of others; one who is fierce toward the cattle of others but not toward his own cattle;
one who is fierce toward both his own cattle and the cattle of others; and one who is fierce neither toward his own cattle nor toward the cattle of others.
These, monks, are the four oxen. Even so, monks, there are four types of persons existing in the world who are like oxen.
"In the world," and so forth—this was spoken by the Blessed One.
Regarding the *Kesi Sutta* in the *Kesivagga*: friend, with reference to whom, on account of what matter, and in what manner was the first *Kesi Sutta* spoken by the Blessed One?
“Vi—this, Bhante, was spoken concerning the trainer of horses, Kesi.
‘Bhante, the Blessed One is the unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed;
but how, Bhante, does the Blessed One train a person to be tamed? It was with reference to this matter, Kesi, that I said: ‘I, Kesi, [train] a person to be tamed...’”
"I discipline them gently; I discipline them harshly; I discipline them both gently and harshly. In this regard, Kesi, here is what is gentle:
'Such is bodily good conduct, such is the result of bodily good conduct; such is verbal good conduct, such is the result of verbal good conduct;
such is mental good conduct, such is the result of mental good conduct; such are the devas, such are human beings'—thus it was spoken by the Blessed One and so forth."
“You are indeed renowned, Kesi, as a trainer of horses to be tamed. But how, Kesi, do you train a horse to be tamed?
“Venerable sir, I train a horse to be tamed with gentleness, I train it with harshness, and I train it with both gentleness and harshness.

“If, Kesi, your horse to be tamed does not submit to training through gentleness, nor does it submit to training through harshness, nor does it submit to training through both gentleness and harshness, what do you do with it?”
“But, Bhante, the Blessed One is the unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed.
How, Bhante, does the Blessed One tame a man to be tamed?”—“Bhante, taking life is not permitted for the Blessed One; yet the Blessed One says, ‘I shall strike him with my hair.
(Attānuvādasutta)
Pu: But, friend, how was the first discourse on self-reproach in the *Bhayavagga* spoken by the Blessed One?
Vi: Venerable sir, in the *Bhayavagga*, the first discourse on self-reproach was spoken thus: “Monks, there are these four fears. Which four?
The fear of self-reproach, the fear of reproach by others, the fear of punishment, and the fear of a miserable rebirth.”
Thus was it spoken by the Blessed One, beginning with these words.
[From] the *Dhammakathikasutta* (Pu):
"Now, friends, for the increase of what has been heard by the many people, certain suttas have been chanted from the *Aṅguttara Nikāya* as well."

Having extracted it, I shall ask you: Venerable friend, how was the ninth discourse on the preacher (*dhammakathikasutta*) spoken by the Blessed One in the *Puggalavagga* of the *Catukkanipāta* of the *Aṅguttara Nikāya* during the Council?
[Vi]—Bhante, in the *Puggalavagga*, the ninth discourse on the preacher is as follows: "Monks, there are these four preachers of the Dhamma."
“What four? Here, monks, a certain Dhamma-preacher speaks little and what is irrelevant, and his assembly is not skilled in distinguishing what is relevant from what is irrelevant.
Such a Dhamma-preacher, monks, is reckoned as a ‘Dhamma-preacher’ only in relation to such an assembly. Thus it was spoken by the Blessed One, and so forth.
Pu: But, friend, how was the seventh discourse on illness spoken by the Blessed One in the Chapter on the Faculties? Vi:
Regarding the seventh discourse on illness, venerable sir: "Bhikkhus, there are these two kinds of illness. Which two? Bodily illness and..."
And there is mental disease. Monks, beings are seen who, though afflicted by physical disease,
claim health for one year, two years, three years, four years, five years, ten years,
twenty years, thirty years, forty years, or even fifty years.
"Those who claim to possess health for even a hundred years, or even more than a hundred years— those beings, monks,
are very rare in the world who can claim to be healthy for even a moment from mental disease, except for those whose taints are destroyed.
Thus it was spoken by the Blessed One, and so forth.
“Bhikkhus, there are these four diseases for one who has gone forth.
*Yuganaddhasutta*:
Friends, where, concerning whom, by whom, and how was the tenth discourse in the *Paṭipadāvagga*, the *Yuganaddhasutta*, spoken?
"Vi— Venerable sir, regarding a number of bhikkhus at Kosambī, it was said by the Venerable Elder Ānanda, the Dhamma-treasurer, beginning with: 'Friends,
whatever bhikkhu or bhikkhunī declares the attainment of arahantship in my presence, all of them have done so by means of one or another of the four paths.'"
Pu: But, friend, how was the second *Pāṭibhogasutta* spoken by the Blessed One in the *Brāhmaṇavagga*? Vi:
Venerable sir, in the *Brāhmaṇavagga*, the second *Pāṭibhogasutta* states: “Bhikkhus, there are four things for which there is no guarantor...”
"Is there anyone—a recluse, a brahmin, a deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world—who can be a guarantor?
This and more was spoken by the Blessed One.
(The Sutasutta)
Pu—In that very context, friends, where, concerning whom, on what subject, and how was the third Discourse on What Was Heard spoken by the Blessed One?
Vi—It was spoken, venerable sir, at Rājagaha, concerning the brahmin Vassakāra, the chief minister of Magadha.
The brahmin Vassakāra, the chief minister of Magadha, said this to the Blessed One: “For I, Master Gotama, am one who speaks thus...”
“Whoever holds such a view and speaks of what they have seen, saying, ‘Thus have I seen,’ there is no fault in that.
Whoever speaks of what they have heard, saying, ‘Thus have I heard,’ there is no fault in that. To this, venerable sir, [the Blessed One replied]:
“Brahmin, I do not say that everything seen should be spoken; nor, brahmin, do I say that everything seen...”
“I say, O Brahmin, that not everything heard should be spoken;
I do not say, O Brahmin, that everything heard should be spoken, nor do I say, O Brahmin, that everything heard should not be spoken. Thus it was said by the Blessed One in the *Abhayasutta*.

Pu: Friend, regarding whom and on what occasion was the fourth discourse, the *Abhayasutta*, spoken by the Blessed One in the Brāhmaṇa Chapter of the Catukka Nipāta of the Aṅguttara Nikāya, and how was it spoken?
Vi: Venerable sir, the fourth discourse, the *Abhayasutta*, was spoken in the Brāhmaṇa Chapter concerning the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi.
Venerable sir, the brahmin Jāṇussoṇi said this to the Blessed One: "There is no one who, being subject to death, does not..."
“He is afraid, he does not fall into terror of death. Regarding that matter, venerable sir, the Blessed One spoke thus:
“There is, brahmin, one who, being subject to death, is afraid and falls into terror of death;
but there is, brahmin, another who, being subject to death, is not afraid and does not fall into terror of death,” and so forth.
Pu: But, friend, how was the first *Sotānugata-sutta* in the *Mahāvagga* spoken by the Blessed One? Vi:
Venerable sir, in the *Mahāvagga*, the first *Sotānugata-sutta* begins: “Bhikkhus, regarding those teachings that have entered through the ear...”
"Regarding those things that have been mastered by word, examined by mind, and well-penetrated by view,
four benefits are to be expected"— thus it was spoken by the Blessed One.
This indeed is that Dhamma and Vinaya wherein I formerly practiced the holy life.
*Bhaddiyasutta Pu*:
In the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*, in the *Catukkanipāta*, in the *Mahāvagga*, this is the third *Bhaddiyasutta*. Where, concerning whom, on what subject, and how was it spoken by the Blessed One? [Answer]:
It was spoken, venerable sir, at Vesālī, concerning the Licchavi Bhaddiya. Venerable sir, the Licchavi Bhaddiya...
He said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, I have heard this: 'The ascetic Gotama is a magician who knows a converting magic by which he converts the disciples of other sectarians.

Venerable sir, those who speak thus—'The ascetic Gotama is a magician who knows a converting magic by which he converts the disciples of other sectarians'... [as above] ...do so because they do not wish to misrepresent him."
"Indeed, Bhante, we have come to the Blessed One. Regarding that matter, Bhante, [the Buddha said]: "Come, Bhaddiya!

Do not go by hearsay, do not go by tradition, do not go by mere report, do not go by the authority of the scriptures, do not go by reasoned conjecture, do not go by inferential grounds, do not go by reflection on appearances, do not go by approval based on a view, do not go by the thought 'He is our respected teacher.'"
“Bhaddiya, when you yourself should know: ‘These states are unwholesome; these states are blameworthy;
these states are censured by the wise; these states, when fully undertaken and practiced, lead to harm and suffering,’ then, Bhaddiya, you should abandon them.
Thus it was spoken by the Blessed One, and so forth.

Pu: "But, friend, when this teaching was delivered, what kind of benefit from hearing the Dhamma did Bhaddiya the Licchavi attain? And how did the Blessed One, after questioning him, resolve that matter?
Vi: "Venerable sir, when this Dhamma-teaching was delivered, Bhaddiya the Licchavi attained the benefit of hearing the Dhamma known as the fruit of stream-entry.
Did I not indeed say to you, Bhaddiya: 'Come, Bhaddiya, [follow me]'?"
"Be my disciple, and I shall be your teacher"— having thus questioned and cross-examined him with these and other words, the Blessed One, venerable sir,
set that statement aside. (From the *Mallikādevīsutta*)
Pu—In that very place, friends, where was the seventh discourse, the *Mallikādevīsutta*, spoken by the Blessed One; concerning whom, on what subject, and in what manner was it spoken?
Vi—It was spoken, venerable sir, at Sāvatthī, concerning Queen Mallikā. Venerable sir, Queen Mallikā said this to the Blessed One:
“What, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the reason, why here some woman is ugly?”
She is ill-favored and very ugly to behold; she is poor, possessing little, with few enjoyments, and of low status...

[as before] ...But what, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the reason, why here some woman is beautiful, lovely to behold, pleasing, endowed with the highest excellence of complexion, and wealthy, possessing great riches and great enjoyments?

"And they are of great influence. Venerable sir, regarding that matter, it was spoken by the Blessed One beginning with: "In this case, Mallikā, a woman is prone to anger and full of distress," and so forth.
This is the *Dasakammasutta*.

Pu: Friend, how was the fourth discourse on the ten actions (*dasakammasutta*) spoken by the Blessed One in the *Sappurisavagga* (Chapter on the True Person) within the *Catukkanipāta* (Book of Fours) of the *Aṅguttaranikāya*?
Vi: Venerable sir, in the *Sappurisavagga*, the fourth discourse on the ten actions is thus:
“Monks, I will teach you the untrue person and one worse than an untrue person, and the true person and one better than a true person.”
"Listen to that and attend to it well"—thus was it spoken by the Blessed One, beginning with these words.
Regarding the *Parisāsutta*:
Friend, how was the first discourse on assemblies (*parisāsutta*) spoken by the Blessed One right there in that section of the assembly?
In the *Parisāvagga*, monks, the first discourse on assemblies (*parisāsutta*) states: "Monks, there are these four defilers of an assembly.
What four? A monk who is immoral and of evil character is a defiler of an assembly; a nun who is immoral and of evil character is a defiler of an assembly;
a lay follower who is immoral and of evil character is a defiler of an assembly..."

“Monks, a female lay follower who is immoral and of evil character is a defiler of the assembly. These, monks, are the four defilers of the assembly,” thus it was spoken by the Blessed One, beginning with these words.
(From the *Sekhabalavagga*)
**Saṃkhittasutta Pu:** But, friend, in the Pañcakanipāta, in the first Saikhabalavagga, where, concerning whom, and how was the first *Saṃkhittasutta* spoken by the Blessed One?
**Vi:** At Sāvatthī, venerable sir, concerning a number of bhikkhus: "Bhikkhus, there are these five powers of one in training (*sekhabala*)."
“What are the five? The power of faith, the power of moral shame, the power of moral dread, the power of energy, and the power of wisdom.
These, monks, are the five powers of one in training. Thus it was spoken by the Blessed One in the *Dukkhasutta*.
Pu: "Friend, how was the third Discourse on Suffering spoken by the Blessed One right there?

Vi: "Venerable sir, the third Discourse on Suffering is thus: 'Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu endowed with five qualities dwells in suffering in this very life—with vexation, distress, and fever—and with the breakup of the body..."
"Beyond death, a miserable destination is to be expected. By which five?
Here, monks, a monk is faithless, he is shameless, he is unafraid of wrongdoing, he is lazy, and he is of poor wisdom. Thus it was spoken by the Blessed One in the *Samāpatti-sutta*.
Pu: Friend, how was the sixth Discourse on Attainment spoken by the Blessed One?
Vi: Regarding the sixth Discourse on Attainment, Bhante:
"Monks, as long as faith is established toward wholesome states, there is no attainment of the unwholesome. But when, monks, faith has disappeared..."
“...when one stands overwhelmed by lack of faith, then there is the attainment of the unwholesome,” so it was spoken by the Blessed One, and so forth.
[Question:
Friend, how was the seventh discourse on sensual pleasures (*kāmasutta*) spoken by the Blessed One right there?
VI—The seventh discourse on sensual pleasures (*kāmasutta*), spoken by the Blessed One beginning with: “Bhikkhus, for the most part beings dally in sensual pleasures.
‘A clansman has gone forth from the home life into homelessness, having abandoned the burden of the household,’ it is sufficient to say, ‘This clansman has gone forth out of faith. Thus it was said.
The Discourse on the Bases of Liberation (Vimuttāyatanasutta). How was the sixth discourse in the Pañcaṅgika-vagga of the Pañcaka-nipāta in the Aṅguttara Nikāya spoken by the Blessed One?
[Venerable: "Bhante, in the Pañcaṅgika-vagga, the sixth discourse, the Vimuttāyatanasutta, states: 'Monks, there are these five bases of liberation.'"
"Wherein, for a bhikkhu dwelling diligent, ardent, and resolute, the mind not yet liberated becomes liberated,
the taints not yet exhausted reach exhaustion, or the unsurpassed security from bondage not yet attained is reached"—
thus it was spoken by the Blessed One, and so forth.
Caṅkamasutta (Pu) — In that very place, friend, how was the ninth Discourse on the Walking Path spoken by the Blessed One?
(Vi) — The ninth, Bhante, is the Discourse on the Walking Path: "Bhikkhus, there are these five benefits in the walking path. Which five?"
“He is able to endure travel; he is able to endure exertion; he has little illness;
what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and tasted is properly digested; and the concentration attained while walking is long-lasting.
These, monks, are the five benefits of walking meditation. Thus, venerable sir, was it spoken by the Blessed One.
Question: Friend, as for the first *Sumanasutta* in the *Sumanavagga*, where was it spoken by the Blessed One, concerning whom, on what occasion, and how was it spoken? Answer:
It was spoken, venerable sir, at Sāvatthī, concerning the princess Sumanā. Venerable sir, [it concerns] the princess Sumanā.
He said this to the Blessed One: "Suppose, Bhante, there were two disciples of the Blessed One here who were equal in faith, equal in virtue, and equal in wisdom;
yet one was a giver and the other was not a giver. When their bodies broke up after death, they might both be reborn in a happy destination, a heavenly world.
But, Bhante, between them as devas, would there be any distinction? Would there be any difference? Regarding that matter, Bhante...
“Whosoever was the giver of jasmine flowers surpasses us, who were non-givers, now that he has become a god, in five respects:
by celestial lifespan, by celestial beauty, by celestial happiness, by celestial fame, and by celestial sovereignty.
Whosoever was the giver of jasmine flowers surpasses us, who were non-givers, now that he has become a god, in these five respects.”
"Thus, venerable sir, has it been spoken by the Blessed One:
'Just as the stainless moon, moving through the expanse of space,
outshines with its radiance all the hosts of stars in the world;'"
In the same way, a person endowed with virtue and faith outshines all those in the world who are miserly through their generosity. —
*Uggahasutta*
Pu—Friend, in that very place, where, concerning whom, on what subject, and how was the third *Uggahasutta* spoken by the Blessed One?
Vi—Venerable sir, the third *Uggahasutta* was spoken at Bhaddiya concerning Uggaha, the grandson of Meṇḍaka.
Venerable sir, Uggaha, the grandson of Meṇḍaka, said this to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, these young women of mine [are going] to their husbands’ families...”

“They will go; may the Blessed One exhort them, may the Blessed One instruct them, so that it may be for their welfare and happiness for a long time. Regarding this matter, venerable sir, [the Blessed One said]: “Therefore, young women, you should train yourselves thus:
‘When our parents, desiring our good, seeking our welfare, and compassionate toward us, give us away to a husband...’”
“Out of compassion, we shall rise before him and retire after him;

we shall be obedient to his commands, pleasant in our conduct, and sweet in our speech. “In this way, young women should train yourselves,” thus it was spoken by the Blessed One in the *Sīhasenāpati-sutta*.

Pu—In the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*, in the *Pañcaka Nipāta*, in the *Sumanavagga*, the fourth discourse, the *Sīhasenāpati Sutta*: where, concerning whom, on what subject, and how was it spoken by the Blessed One?
Vi—It was spoken, venerable sir, at Vesālī, concerning the general Sīha. The general Sīha, venerable sir, said this to the Blessed One:
“Is it possible, venerable sir, to point out the fruit of giving as something visible here and now? Regarding that, venerable sir...
Regarding the subject matter, the Blessed One spoke thus: "It is possible, Sīha; one who gives, Sīha, a donor, a lord of giving, becomes dear and pleasing to many people," and so forth.
Pu: In that very same context, friend, how was the sixth discourse on timely giving (*kāladāna-sutta*) spoken by the Blessed One?
VI—The sixth, Bhante, is the Sutta on Timely Gifts: “Monks, there are these five timely gifts.
What are the five? One gives a gift to a newcomer; one gives a gift to a traveler; one gives a gift to the sick; one gives a gift during a famine;
and when there are new crops and new fruits, one first establishes them with those who are virtuous.”
“Monks, these indeed are the five timely gifts,” thus was it spoken by the Blessed One, beginning with these words.
Pu: In that very same place, friends, how was the seventh discourse on food (Bhojanasutta) spoken by the Blessed One?
VI—The seventh discourse on food: "Monks, when a donor gives food, he gives five things to the recipients.
What are the five? He gives life, he gives beauty, he gives happiness, he gives strength, and he gives eloquence.
Having given life, he becomes a partaker of life, whether divine or human."
Thus was it spoken by the Blessed One, beginning with these words.
Regarding the *Puttasutta*:
"In that same place, friends, how was the ninth discourse on children (*puttasutta*) spoken by the Blessed One?"
Vi—The ninth, O Venerable Sir, is the *Puttasutta*. It was spoken by the Blessed One beginning with: "Bhikkhus, seeing five grounds, parents desire a son to be born into their family.

What are the five? 'He will support us when we are supported; he will perform our duties; the lineage of the family will endure for long; he will take charge of the inheritance. This is the *Nāradasutta*.
Pu—Friend, where, concerning whom, on what subject, by whom, and in what manner was the tenth discourse in the Muṇḍarājavagga, the Nāradasutta, spoken?
Vi—It was spoken, venerable sir, at Pāṭaliputta, concerning King Muṇḍa.
Venerable sir, King Muṇḍa’s Queen Bhaddā, who was dear and beloved to him, had passed away. Because Queen Bhaddā, his dear and beloved wife, had passed away, he neither...
He neither bathed nor anointed himself, nor did he eat his meals, nor did he attend to his business;
day and night he remained utterly infatuated with Queen Bhaddā’s body. Regarding that matter, venerable sir, [the Blessed One said]:
"Great King, there are these five things that cannot be obtained by an ascetic or a brahmin, by a god, by Māra, by Brahmā, or by anyone in the world."
"Venerable sir, this has been taught by the Venerable Elder Nārada to King Pasenadi of Kosala according to the method taught by the Blessed One.
What, venerable sir, is the name of this discourse on the Dhamma?
Truly, venerable sir, it is 'The Extractor of the Arrow of Sorrow.'"

Friend, how was the fourth Discourse on the Occasion (*Samayasutta Pu*) spoken by the Blessed One in the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*, in the *Pañcaka Nipāta*, in the section on the Hindrances (*Nīvaraṇavagga*)?
Venerable sir, in the section on the Hindrances, the fourth Discourse on the Occasion states: "Monks, there are these five non-occasions for striving."
"What are the five? Here, monks, a monk is aged, overcome by old age.
This, monks, is the first unfavorable time for striving," and so forth, as spoken by the Blessed One.
*Ṭhānasutta*.
Pu—Friend, how was the seventh discourse on the stations (ṭhānasutta) spoken by the Blessed One?

Vi—Venerable sir, the seventh discourse on the stations is as follows: “Bhikkhus, these five stations should be frequently reflected upon by a woman or a man, whether a householder or one gone forth. Which five? ‘I am subject to aging;’”
"One has not transcended old age"— this must be frequently reflected upon by a woman or a man, by one who is a householder or one who has gone forth.
Thus it was spoken by the Blessed One in the *Dhammavihārīsutta*.
Pu: But, friend, how was the third discourse on dwelling in the Dhamma (*dhammavihārisutta*) spoken by the Blessed One in the Chapter on Warriors (*yodhājīvavagga*)?
Vi: In the Chapter on Warriors, venerable sir, the third discourse on dwelling in the Dhamma is as follows:

"In this case, a bhikkhu masters the Dhamma—the discourses (*sutta*), mixed prose and verse (*geyya*), expositions (*veyyākaraṇa*), verses (*gāthā*), inspired utterances (*udāna*), sayings in prose and verse (*itivuttaka*), birth stories (*jātaka*), marvelous qualities (*abbhutadhamma*)."
"The Vedalla: he spends his day with that study of the Dhamma, neglects seclusion, and does not devote himself to internal tranquility of mind.
This, bhikkhus, is called a bhikkhu who is full of textual learning but does not dwell in the Dhamma.
Thus, venerable sir, it was spoken by the Blessed One.
"Venerable sir, it is said, 'one who dwells in the Dhamma, one who dwells in the Dhamma. In what way, venerable sir, is a bhikkhu one who dwells in the Dhamma?

The Second Discourse on Future Perils (Dutiya-anāgata-bhaya-sutta), the eighth in the Chapter on Warriors (Yodhājīva-vagga) of the Fivefold Collection (Pañcaka-nipāta) in the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*, was spoken by the Blessed One as follows: [The discourse continues with the Buddha explaining the various future perils that threaten the Sangha if they neglect the practice of the Dhamma.]
In the *Yodhājīva-vagga*, venerable sir, the eighth discourse, the *Dutiya-anāgata-bhaya-sutta*, was spoken by the Blessed One beginning with these words:
"Bhikkhus, seeing these five future perils, it is sufficient for a bhikkhu to dwell diligent, ardent, and resolute, for the attainment of the unattained,
for the reaching of the unreached, for the realization of the unrealized."
Pu – In that very place, friend, how was the ninth Discourse on Future Dangers (Tatiya-anāgata-bhaya-sutta) spoken by the Blessed One?
Vi – In that very place, venerable sir, the ninth Discourse on Future Dangers was spoken thus: “Monks, there are these five future dangers.”
"Those [faults] which have not yet arisen but will arise in the future must be recognized by you;
having recognized them, you must strive for their abandonment. "And what, monks, are the five?

In the future, monks, there will be monks who have not developed the body, have not developed virtue, have not developed the mind, and have not developed wisdom. Thus it was spoken by the Blessed One, beginning with these words.
The Fourth Discourse on Future Dangers (Catuttha-anāgata-bhaya-sutta).

Pu: Venerable friend, how was the tenth discourse in the Chapter on Warriors (Yodhājīva-vagga) of the Section of Fives (Pañcaka-nipāta) in the Aṅguttara Nikāya—the Fourth Discourse on Future Dangers—spoken by the Blessed One?
Vi: Venerable sir, in the Chapter on Warriors, the tenth discourse, the Fourth Discourse on Future Dangers, [begins]: "Bhikkhus, there are these five future dangers..."
“Future dangers that have not yet arisen will arise in the future;
you must be awake to them, and having become awake, you must strive for their abandonment. Thus it was spoken by the Blessed One, beginning with these words, in the Kakudha-vagga.
Friend, how was the ninth discourse, the *Sīhasutta*, spoken by the Blessed One in the *Kakudha-vagga*?
Venerable sir, in the *Kakudha-vagga*, the ninth discourse, the *Sīhasutta*, [begins]: "Bhikkhus, in the evening time, the lion, the king of beasts..."
“From his lair he emerges; having emerged from his lair, he stretches; having stretched, he surveys the four quarters all around;
having surveyed the four quarters all around, he roars three times the lion’s roar”—thus it was spoken by the Blessed One in the *Andhakavindavagga*.
Friend, how was the first *Kulūpaka-sutta* spoken by the Blessed One in the *Andhakavinda-vagga*?
Venerable sir, in the *Andhakavinda-vagga*, the first *Kulūpaka-sutta* [begins]: "Bhikkhus, by five qualities..."

“Bhante, it has been said by the Blessed One in the *Andhakavinda Sutta*: ‘A bhikkhu who frequents families and is possessed of such [faults] becomes unloved and displeasing to those families, and is neither respected nor esteemed. Thus was it spoken by the Blessed One.
Pu: Friend, in that very place, where, concerning whom, and how was the fourth *Andhakavinda Sutta* spoken by the Blessed One?
Vi: Lord, at Andhakavinda in Magadha, concerning the Venerable Ānanda, [he said]:
"Ānanda, those bhikkhus who are new, recently gone forth, having only lately come to this Dhamma and Vinaya—those bhikkhus, Ānanda, should be encouraged in five things..."
“They should be encouraged, established, and settled,” thus it was spoken by the Blessed One in the *Satisūpaṭṭhitasutta* of the *Gilānavagga*.
Pu: Friend, how was the second Discourse on Mindfulness Being Well-Established (*Satisūpaṭṭhitasutta*) spoken by the Blessed One in the *Pañcakanipāta*, in the *Gilānavagga* of the *Aṅguttaranikāya*?
Vi: Venerable sir, in the *Gilānavagga*, the second Discourse on Mindfulness Being Well-Established states:
"Bhikkhus, whatever bhikkhu or bhikkhunī develops five things and cultivates five things, for them there are two fruits..."
"One of two fruits may be expected: either final knowledge in this very life, or, if there is a residue remaining, the state of a non-returner.
"Which five? Here, monks, a monk’s mindfulness is established precisely within himself," and so forth—thus it was spoken by the Blessed One.
This is the *Upaṭṭhākasutta*.
Pu—Friend, how was the third Discourse on the Attendant spoken by the Blessed One?
Vi—Venerable sir, the third Discourse on the Attendant is thus: "Bhikkhus, a patient who possesses five qualities is difficult to attend to.
Which five? He does what is unsuitable; he does not know moderation regarding what is suitable; [he does not take] medicine..."
“It is not to be indulged in,” thus it was spoken by the Blessed One, and so forth.
Regarding the *Anāyussā-sutta*:
Friend, how was the fifth discourse, the *Anāyussā-sutta*, spoken by the Blessed One?
Vi—The fifth, Bhante, is the *Anāyussasutta*, spoken by the Blessed One beginning with: “Bhikkhus, there are these five things that shorten life.
Which five? One acts in an unsuitable manner; one does not know moderation regarding what is suitable;
one eats indigestible food; one wanders at improper times; and one does not live the holy life. These, bhikkhus, are the five things that shorten life. Thus it was said.
The Discourse on the Happiness of a Recluse (Samaṇasukhasutta) Pu: Friend, how was the eighth discourse on the happiness of a recluse spoken by the Blessed One? Vi:
Venerable sir, the eighth discourse on the happiness of a recluse is as follows: "Monks, there are these five sufferings of a recluse. Which five?"
There are five, monks: here a monk is not content with any kind of robe,
he is not content with any kind of almsfood, he is not content with any kind of lodging,
he is not content with any kind of medicinal requisites for the sick, and he leads the holy life without delight.
“Monks, these indeed are the five sufferings of a recluse,” thus it was spoken by the Blessed One, beginning with these words.
[From the] *Byasanasutta*:
“Friend, how was the tenth discourse on misfortune (*byasanasutta*) spoken by the Blessed One right there?”
Vi—The Tenth Discourse on Calamities (*Byasanasutta*). "Monks, there are these five calamities. Which five?

The calamity of relatives, the calamity of wealth, the calamity of illness, the calamity of moral failure, and the calamity of wrong view"—thus was it spoken by the Blessed One, beginning with these words, in the *Rājavagga*.
Friend, how was the sixth Discourse on Aspiration (Patthanāsutta) spoken by the Blessed One in the Chapter on Kings (Rājavagga)?
Venerable sir, in the Chapter on Kings, the sixth Discourse on Aspiration is as follows: “Bhikkhus, when one is endowed with five factors...”
