“‘The eldest son of a consecrated Kṣatriya king aspires to the vice-regency’”—thus was it spoken by the Blessed One.
Regarding the *Sappurisadānasutta* (Discourse on the Gift of a True Person) in the *Tikaṇḍakīvagga*: friends, how was the eighth discourse, the *Sappurisadānasutta*, spoken by the Blessed One?

In the *Vi-tikaṇḍakī-vagga*, venerable sir, the eighth discourse, the *Sappurisadānasutta*, was spoken by the Blessed One as follows: "Monks, there are these five gifts of a true person (*sappurisa*).
What are the five? One gives a gift with faith; one gives a gift respectfully; one gives a gift at the proper time;
one gives a gift with a mind of assistance; and one gives a gift without harming oneself or others. Thus it was said by the Blessed One.
Saddhammavagga:
First Discourse on the Certainty of Rightness. Questioner:
But, friend, how was the first discourse on the certainty of rightness spoken by the Blessed One in the Saddhamma Chapter?
Venerable sir, in the *Saddhammavagga*, the first discourse, the *Sammattaniyāmasutta*, was spoken by the Blessed One as follows:
"Bhikkhus, one who possesses five qualities—even Sunakkhatta—is incapable of entering upon the certainty of rightness regarding wholesome states.
Which five? He disparages the teacher, he disparages the discourse, and he disparages himself," and so forth.
Pu: Friend, how was the fourth Discourse on the Corruption of the True Dharma spoken by the Blessed One in that very place? Vi:
Venerable sir, in that very place the fourth Discourse on the Corruption of the True Dharma was spoken as follows: "Bhikkhus, there are these five things..."
They lead to the confusion and disappearance of the true Dhamma. What are the five? Here, monks, monks do not listen to the Dhamma respectfully;
they do not master the Dhamma respectfully; they do not retain the Dhamma respectfully;
they do not examine the meaning of the Dhammas they have retained respectfully; and having understood the meaning, they do not [practice] respectfully.
"Having understood the Dhamma, they practice in accordance with the Dhamma. "Monks, these five things lead to the confusion and disappearance of the true Dhamma," so it was said by the Blessed One.
This concludes the Second Discourse on the Confusion of the True Dhamma.
Pu: "Friend, how was the fifth discourse on the second corruption of the true Dhamma spoken by the Blessed One?
Vi: "In that very place, Bhante, the fifth discourse on the second corruption of the true Dhamma was spoken thus:
'Monks, there are these five things that lead to the corruption and disappearance of the true Dhamma. What are the five? Here, monks, monks..."
“They do not master the Dhamma— the discourses, mixed prose and verse, expositions, verses, inspired utterances,

legends, birth stories, marvelous qualities, and questions-and-answers. This, monks, is the first factor that leads to the confusion and disappearance of the true Dhamma,” thus it was spoken by the Blessed One, and so forth.
Pu: Friend, how was the sixth discourse on the confusion of the true Dhamma spoken by the Blessed One right there? Vi:
Venerable sir, the sixth discourse on the confusion of the true Dhamma was spoken right there by the Blessed One thus: "Bhikkhus, there are these five things..."
They lead to the confusion and disappearance of the true Dhamma. What are the five?
Here, monks, monks master discourses that have been wrongly grasped, with words and phrasing poorly set down.
Monks, when words and phrasing are poorly set down, the meaning is also wrongly interpreted. This, monks, is the first factor for the confusion of the true Dhamma.
"It leads to confusion and disappearance"— thus was it spoken by the Blessed One, and so forth.

Regarding the *Dukkathāsutta* (The Discourse on Bad Talk) in the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*, friends, in the *Pañcaka Nipāta*, in the *Saddhamma Vagga*, how was the seventh discourse, the *Dukkathāsutta*, spoken by the Blessed One?
In the *Saddhamma-vagga*, monks, the seventh discourse is the *Dukkathā-sutta*: "Monks, for five types of persons, speaking about them in comparison with another person is ill-spoken.
Which five? Monks, for one who lacks faith, speaking about faith is ill-spoken;
for one who is immoral, speaking about virtue is ill-spoken; for one who is unlearned, speaking about great learning..."
“Talk on generosity is ill-spoken for one who is stingy; talk on wisdom is ill-spoken for one who lacks wisdom”—this and more was spoken by the Blessed One.
Pu: In that very same context, friends, where, concerning whom, on what matter, and how was the ninth discourse, the Udāyīsutta, spoken by the Blessed One?
At Kosambī, venerable sir, this was said concerning the Venerable Udāyī.

The Venerable Udāyī, venerable sir, was sitting surrounded by a large assembly of householders, teaching the Dhamma. The Venerable Ānanda saw the Venerable Udāyī sitting surrounded by a large assembly of householders, teaching the Dhamma. Having seen him, he approached the Blessed One.
He approached him, and having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.

As he was sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, the Venerable Udāyī is teaching the Dhamma surrounded by a large assembly of householders. Regarding that matter, venerable sir, [the Blessed One said]: "Ānanda, it is not easy for others..."
"Ānanda, when teaching the Dhamma to others, one who teaches the Dhamma to others should teach the Dhamma to them after establishing five qualities within oneself"—
thus it was spoken by the Blessed One, beginning with these words.
(The Chapter on Resentment)
Pu: But, friend, how was the first Discourse on the Removal of Resentment spoken by the Blessed One in the Chapter on Resentment?
Vi: Venerable sir, in the Chapter on Resentment, the first Discourse on the Removal of Resentment is as follows: “Bhikkhus, there are these five ways of removing resentment.”
"Wherever resentment has arisen in a bhikkhu, it must be entirely dispelled. Which five?
Bhikkhus, toward whatever person resentment might arise, loving-kindness (*mettā*) should be cultivated toward that person; in this way, resentment toward that person is to be dispelled.
Thus it was spoken by the Blessed One, and so forth.
Friend, how was the fifth sutta in the Upāsaka-vagga, the Caṇḍāla-sutta, spoken by the Blessed One?
Vi—In the *Upāsakavagga*, venerable sir, the fifth discourse, the *Caṇḍālasutta*, was spoken by the Blessed One as follows:
“Bhikkhus, a lay follower endowed with five qualities is a caṇḍāla among lay followers, a stain among lay followers, and one who is despised among lay followers,” and so forth.
This is the *Pītisutta*.
Pu: Friend, regarding that very same sixth Discourse on Rapture (*pītisutta*), where, concerning whom, and how was it spoken by the Blessed One?
Vi: Venerable sir, the sixth Discourse on Rapture was spoken at Sāvatthī concerning the householder Anāthapiṇḍika:
“Householder, you have attended upon the Saṅgha of bhikkhus with robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.”
“Householder, you should not be satisfied with merely this much: ‘We have attended to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus with robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick.
Therefore, householder, you should train yourself thus: ‘How can we dwell from time to time, having attained the rapture of seclusion?’”
Thus it was spoken by the Blessed One, beginning with these words.
Regarding the *Vaṇijjāsutta*:
"In that very place, friends, how was the seventh discourse on trade spoken by the Blessed One?"
"Vi—In that very place, venerable sir, the seventh Discourse on Trades was spoken by the Blessed One thus: 'Monks, there are these five trades that should not be practiced by a lay follower.
Which five? Trade in weapons, trade in living beings, trade in meat, trade in intoxicants, and trade in poisons.
These, monks, are the five trades that should not be practiced by a lay follower. Thus, venerable sir, it was spoken by the Blessed One.
Gavesīsutta (Pu):
"Friend, where, concerning whom, on what subject, and how was the tenth Gavesīsutta spoken by the Blessed One?
(Vi): "Venerable sir, the tenth Gavesīsutta was spoken among the Kosalans, concerning the Venerable Ānanda Thera, the Dhamma-treasurer."
This was said with reference to that. Venerable Ānanda Thera, the Dhamma-treasurer, said this to the Blessed One:
“What, venerable sir, is the cause, what is the reason for the Blessed One’s manifestation of a smile? Tathāgatas do not manifest a smile without a reason.
Regarding that matter, venerable sir, [the Blessed One said]: “In the past, Ānanda, in this very place...”
“The city was prosperous, flourishing, populous, and teeming with people;
moreover, Ānanda, the Blessed One Kassapa, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, dwelt in dependence upon that city. Thus it was spoken by the Blessed One in the *Vācāsutta*.
Pu—Friend, how was the eighth discourse on speech (*vācāsutta*) spoken by the Blessed One in the *Brāhmaṇavagga*?
Vi—Venerable sir, in the *Brāhmaṇavagga*, the eighth discourse on speech was spoken thus:
"Bhikkhus, speech endowed with five qualities is well-spoken, not ill-spoken; it is blameless and beyond reproach to the wise. With which five?..."

“Monks, speech endowed with these five factors is well-spoken, not ill-spoken; it is blameless and beyond reproach by the wise: it is spoken at the proper time, it is spoken truthfully, it is spoken gently, it is spoken meaningfully, and it is spoken with a mind of loving-kindness. It is in this way, monks...”
"Venerable sir, it was spoken by the Blessed One.
Friend, how was the ninth discourse on families spoken by the Blessed One right there?"
"Vi—In that very place, Bhante, is the ninth Discourse on Families: 'Monks, when virtuous renunciants visit a family, people there generate much merit through five grounds. What are the five?
Monks, at the time when people see virtuous renunciants visiting their family, their minds..."
“...they inspire confidence; at that time, bhikkhus, that family has entered upon a practice that leads to heaven.
Thus it was spoken by the Blessed One in the Kimilavagga.
Pu: But, friend, how was the second *Dhammassavanasutta* (Discourse on Hearing the Dhamma) spoken by the Blessed One in the Kimila Chapter?
Vi: Venerable sir, in the Kimila Chapter, the second *Dhammassavanasutta* is thus spoken: “Monks, there are these five benefits in hearing the Dhamma.”
“What five? One hears what has not been heard; one clarifies what has been heard; one overcomes doubt; one straightens one’s view;
one’s mind becomes serene. These, monks, are the five benefits of hearing the Dhamma.
Thus, venerable sir, was it spoken by the Blessed One.
In the *Akkosakavagga*,
friends, how was the fifth sutta, the *Akkhantisutta*, spoken by the Blessed One?
“Bhante, in the *Akkosaka-vagga*, this is the fifth discourse on intolerance: ‘Monks, there are these five disadvantages of intolerance.
What are the five? One is disliked and displeasing to many people; one becomes full of enmity; one becomes full of fault-finding; one dies confused;
and with the breakup of the body, after death, one is reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or hell.’”
"...is reborn," and so forth—thus it was spoken by the Blessed One.
Regarding the *Apāsādika Sutta*:
"In that very place, friend, how was the eighth discourse, the *Apāsādika Sutta*, spoken by the Blessed One?"
Vi—Right there, Bhante, is the eighth discourse on what is unlovely: "Monks, there are these five dangers in what is unlovely.
Which five? Those who have no confidence do not gain confidence; some of those who have confidence become otherwise;
the Teacher’s instruction is not carried out; later generations follow that example; and one's own mind does not become confident. These..."
“Monks, there are these five disadvantages in what is uninspiring,” so it was said by the Blessed One, beginning with these words.
(From the *Āvāsika-vagga*,
the *Āvāsika-sutta*).
Pu: But, friend, how was the first *āvāsika-sutta* (resident-monk discourse) in the *Āvāsika-vagga* spoken by the Blessed One?
Vi: Venerable sir, in the *Āvāsika-vagga*, the first *āvāsika-sutta* is as follows: "Bhikkhus, a resident monk endowed with five qualities is not worthy of being cultivated.
With which five? He is not perfect in deportment, nor is he perfect in conduct..."
"He is not learned, nor is he one who retains what he has heard; he does not practice seclusion, nor does he delight in seclusion;
he is not a man of beautiful speech, nor is he skilled in speaking beautifully; he is of poor wisdom, dull, and muddle-headed.
Possessing these five qualities, monks, a resident monk is not worthy of being cultivated. Thus it was spoken by the Blessed One, beginning with these words.
Pu: Friend, how was the seventh discourse on those deserving of dispraise spoken by the Blessed One in that very place? Vi:
Venerable sir, in that very place the seventh discourse on those deserving of dispraise was spoken thus: “Bhikkhus, one endowed with five qualities... [as above]”
The resident monk is placed in hell exactly as he was deposited there. By what five [qualities]?
Without investigating and without scrutinizing, he speaks in praise of one who deserves dispraise; without investigating and without scrutinizing, he speaks in dispraise of one who deserves praise;
he is envious of the residence and greedy for the residence; he is envious of families and greedy for families; he misappropriates what has been given in faith.
"He brings about downfall. Monks, a resident monk endowed with these five qualities is placed in hell as if carried there.
Thus it was spoken by the Blessed One, beginning with these words, in the *Duccaritavagga*.
Pu: But, friend, how was the first Discourse on Misconduct spoken by the Blessed One in the Chapter on Misconduct? Vi:
Venerable sir, in the Chapter on Misconduct, the first Discourse on Misconduct was spoken thus: "Monks, there are these five dangers in misconduct."
"What are the five? One blames oneself; the wise, having investigated, censure one;
an evil reputation spreads abroad; one dies confused; and with the breakup of the body, after death, one reappears in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or hell.
These, monks, are the five dangers in misconduct. Thus it was spoken by the Blessed One, and so forth.
Pu: Friend, how was the ninth Discourse on the Cemetery (Sivathikasutta) spoken by the Blessed One right there? Vi:
Venerable sir, right there the ninth Discourse on the Cemetery was spoken thus: “Bhikkhus, there are these five dangers in a cemetery.”
“What five? It is impure, foul-smelling, terrifying, an abode for wild non-human beings, and a place where many people weep.
These, monks, are the five dangers in a charnel ground,” thus it was spoken by the Blessed One, and so forth.
